claims.text: Adding additional elements to a low-entropy platinum-group-metal catalyst increases its mixing entropy.
Increased mixing entropy favors formation of a multielement alloy phase by lowering the Gibbs free energy and predicted alloy-formation temperature.
Increasing mixing entropy produces a homogeneous, entropy-stabilized HEA phase.
The resulting alloy contains a random distribution of dissimilar metal atoms.
The HEA phase provides a uniform spatial distribution of active sites.
Dissimilar species in high-entropy catalysts generate diverse active sites and tunable local electronic structures.
The diverse active sites provide balanced or moderate binding energies for key ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Tailoring the local electronic structure enables optimal adsorption and transformation of ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Ethanol oxidation proceeds through a 12-electron and 12-proton transfer process.
A balance between electron donation and acceptance improves ethanol-oxidation reaction rates.
The same balance between electron donation and acceptance improves catalyst durability.
The HEA catalyst will have a lower ethanol-oxidation onset potential than the bimetallic baseline.
The HEA catalyst will produce a higher ethanol-oxidation current density than the bimetallic baseline.
The HEA catalyst will have better long-term stability than the bimetallic baseline.
The proposed effect applies under standard alkaline ethanol-oxidation conditions at moderate synthesis or operating temperatures.
Temperatures below the predicted alloy-formation temperature are thermodynamically favorable for alloy formation.
Conditions that promote phase segregation will diminish the catalytic benefits attributed to the HEA.
Extremely high temperatures may diminish HEA benefits by promoting phase segregation.

contradictions.description: The conditions field identifies temperatures below the predicted alloy-formation temperature as favorable, whereas the entropy-based mechanism and cited thermodynamics make the alloy phase increasingly favorable with increasing temperature and describe a reduced formation temperature as enabling alloy formation.
